talking_points: AI agents are moving inside the software companies already use: Salesforce now runs 37 sales tasks through Claude.
Much of the AI build-out is paid for with borrowed money, which is why lenders are watching demand so closely.
New AI risks create new startups within months, like AIR raising $50M to vet the add-ons agents install.

industry.headline: Salesforce puts 37 sales workflows directly inside Claude
industry.standfirst: The CRM giant is betting that salespeople would rather ask an AI than click through dashboards.
paragraphs: Salesforce has released a beta plugin that lets sales teams run 37 everyday workflows, from researching an account to preparing for a call or reviewing their pipeline, from inside Anthropic's Claude assistant.

The plugin uses each salesperson's existing Salesforce permissions, so the AI can only see what that person could already see. Any change to customer records still needs a human to confirm it before it's saved.

The move reflects a wider shift in enterprise software. Rather than building their own models, established software companies are plugging their data and workflows into the leading AI assistants, betting that the assistant becomes the place where work starts.

concepts.explanation: Software that stores everything a company knows about its customers: contacts, deals, emails and calls. Salesforce is the biggest CRM provider.
An AI system that takes actions, like looking up records or drafting emails, rather than only answering questions.
A design where the AI does the work but pauses for a person to approve risky actions. Think of a junior employee who drafts everything but needs sign-off before sending.

industry.why_it_matters: Partnerships between software platforms and AI labs are creating roles in AI integration and solutions engineering. Being able to explain why a company would partner rather than build is a strong interview point.

finance.headline: JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs line up to lend billions to European AI
finance.standfirst: US banks are bringing the AI debt boom to Europe, despite nerves about how much is being spent.
paragraphs: JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are among the banks preparing to finance billions of dollars of debt for AI projects in Europe, mostly data centres, as the region tries to catch up with the US.
Data centres cost billions to build, and companies increasingly borrow to pay for them rather than using cash or selling shares. Lenders earn interest, while the borrowers keep full ownership.
The risk is timing: the loans assume demand for AI computing keeps growing fast enough for the data centres to earn back their cost. Some investors worry that spending is running ahead of revenue.

concepts.explanation: Raising money by borrowing it and paying interest, like a mortgage. You keep ownership, but you must repay whatever happens.
Raising money by selling part of the company. There's nothing to repay, but the founders own less.
Money spent on long-lasting physical assets such as buildings, chips and servers, as opposed to day-to-day running costs.

finance.why_it_matters: "Is AI a bubble?" is a common interview question. A strong answer notes that AI spending is increasingly debt-funded, which spreads the risk to banks and bond investors.

startups.headline: AIR raises $50M to vet the add-ons AI agents use
startups.standfirst: A security startup is betting that agents' plugins will become the next big attack route.
paragraphs: AI security startup AIR has raised $50 million across two seed rounds to monitor the plugins, tools and skills that companies let their AI agents install.
Agents gain new abilities through add-ons, much like apps on a phone. A malicious or badly built add-on could leak data or take harmful actions, and AIR checks them before companies trust them.

concepts.explanation: A startup's first significant outside funding, usually used to build the product and find early customers.
Protecting against risks that come from third-party code and tools you rely on, not just your own software.

startups.why_it_matters: A new problem appeared and a startup raised money to fix it within months. Spotting that pattern is exactly what interviewers mean by commercial awareness.

code_corner.title: How much of the company did investors buy?
code_corner.intro: When a startup raises money, the size of the round and the valuation tell you how much of the company changed hands. Here's that sum in Python.
walkthrough: def stake_sold(...) defines a reusable function that takes two numbers.
post_money is the company's value right after the new cash arrives: its old value plus the money raised.
The share investors bought is the money they put in divided by the post-money value.
rounds is a dictionary: each name maps to a pair of numbers (a tuple). The underscores in 50_000_000 just make big numbers readable.
The for loop unpacks each pair into raised and pre, and :.1% formats the result as a percentage with one decimal place.
code_corner.try_it: Add a "Series B" round raising $300M at a $2.7B pre-money valuation. What percentage did investors buy?

quiz.scenario: You're in your first week as an analyst at a bank. Your manager asks why a data centre developer might borrow £500M rather than sell shares.
quiz.question: What's the best answer?
options: Borrowing lets the owners keep full ownership, as long as they can make the repayments
Borrowing is always cheaper than any other kind of funding
Selling shares is illegal for infrastructure companies
Loans don't have to be repaid if the project fails
quiz.explanation: Debt keeps ownership intact, which appeals when owners expect the asset to be very valuable. B is tempting, but debt isn't always cheaper: interest rates and repayment risk matter.

quiz.scenario: Your team wants to let an AI agent update customer records in your CRM automatically. A colleague is nervous.
quiz.question: Which design addresses the risk while keeping the time savings?
options: Give the agent admin access so it never gets blocked
Let the agent draft changes, and have a person approve them before they're saved
Turn the agent off and do everything by hand
Only let the agent work at night when nobody is watching
quiz.explanation: That's human-in-the-loop: the agent does the work, and a person signs off on risky actions. A removes the safeguard entirely.
